paras: The Napoleon shooting of Walter G. Drury by Robert K. Scott took place early on 25 December 1880, when Scott, a former Governor of South Carolina living in Napoleon, Ohio, shot and killed Drury, a young drugstore clerk, in a dispute over Scott's drunken son. Scott was charged with murder, and talk of lynching in the town led the sheriff to keep him under militia guard and then move him to the jail at Defiance. Papers across the country carried the story because of Scott's prominence as a Reconstruction governor, and one later item said he had "narrowly escaped lynching."

Scott, aged 56, was a Pennsylvania native who had practiced medicine in Henry County, Ohio, commanded an Ohio regiment in the war, and governed South Carolina before returning to Napoleon. Drury, 23, had lived in Napoleon about six months, clerked in C. A. Keeland's drug store, and was due to be married within days to a young woman from Pittsburg.

On Christmas Eve Scott's son, who had been drinking with Drury and others, avoided his parents' hotel and spent the night in Drury's bed at the store. After a messenger failed to bring the boy home, Scott went to the store and, at about one in the morning, demanded to go to the bedroom. When Drury turned and refused to let him in, Scott fired his revolver, and the ball struck Drury below the left ear and killed him instantly.

Scott gave himself up to the sheriff, who held him at his hotel because the court house and jail had burned, and he was arraigned before a justice of the peace and pleaded not guilty. A coroner's jury found that Drury had died by a pistol shot fired by R. K. Scott. Through the day, according to the Chicago Tribune's correspondent, there were "threats and loose talk about lynching the Governor" among men who had been drinking, and Toledo and Cincinnati dispatches said a militia company guarded the hotel. That evening the sheriff and a large force of assistants took Scott by train to Defiance and placed him in jail; a "large mob of half-drunken men" followed on the same train, but no serious trouble occurred.

Drury's body was taken to Elmore, Ohio, his former home, where the Masons, who had taken charge of it, sent it for burial in the suit meant for his wedding. A preliminary hearing was set for the following Monday at Napoleon, and a later item reported that Scott had been committed to jail at Defiance. No report of the hearing's result or of a trial was found in the coverage.

The story ran first as Toledo and Napoleon wires on 26 and 27 December in the New-York Tribune, Portland Daily Press, Wilmington Daily Republican and Wheeling Register, and in a fuller report by the Chicago Tribune's own correspondent. Headlines generally called it murder, from "Murdered by Ex-Governor Scott" in New York to "An Ex-Governor's Crime" in the Richmond Dispatch, whose subhead read "Threatened with Lynching for the Murder of a Young Man." The Chicago Tribune alone gave Scott's own version at length and treated the lynching talk as the "usual" loose talk of drinking men.

Several papers used the shooting to revisit Scott's Reconstruction record: the Richmond Dispatch called his rule "one of continued corruption," and the Ottawa Free Trader said he had gained "more notoriety" than reputation in South Carolina. The Millheim Journal, in Pennsylvania, called him "the first of the carpet-bag Governors" and quoted the Philadelphia Record on a "suggestive fatality in the misfortunes of the whole line of political spoilsmen in the South." That paper's brief, printed a week after the event, also gave the strongest account of the danger, saying Scott "narrowly escaped lynching" and that the military were called out to restore order.

Scott said the revolver in his overcoat pocket went off by accident as he tried to pass Drury, and the Chicago Tribune noted that no one else witnessed the shooting. The Napoleon wire left open whether he fired "intentionally, or, as he claims, accidentally," while a Toledo dispatch of 26 December said the evidence so far pointed to a fit of anger at Drury's refusal.

bases: An individual, ex-Governor Robert K. Scott, shot and killed Walter G. Drury in a drugstore at Napoleon, Ohio, after which townspeople threatened to lynch Scott while he was held by the sheriff; no crowd violence took place and no paper describes a racial dimension (A1, A3, A4, A6).

accounts.label: Scott's account
accounts.gist: Scott said Drury blocked his way up the stairs and that the revolver in his overcoat pocket went off accidentally as he tried to pass; he said he had no intention of shooting Drury.

accounts.label: Napoleon wire (inquest-day report)
accounts.gist: Drury refused to let Scott into the bedroom, and Scott drew his revolver and fired, 'either intentionally, or, as he claims, accidentally'; the inquest found Drury died by a shot fired by Scott.

accounts.label: Toledo wire, Dec 26
accounts.gist: The evidence so far indicated the deed was done in a fit of anger at Drury's refusal to admit Scott to the room where Drury had taken his intoxicated son.

accounts.label: Townspeople's view (as reported)
accounts.gist: Many in Napoleon discredited Scott's account, claiming the shooting was intentional and the result of a quarrel.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune's correspondent gave Scott's account at length, called the lynching talk 'the usual threats and loose talk' of men who had been drinking, and quoted Scott deploring the affair.
Headlines such as 'Murdered by Ex-Governor Scott' and 'An Ex-Governor's Crime' treated the shooting as murder, and the Richmond Dispatch called Scott's governorship 'one of continued corruption'.
The Millheim Journal called Scott 'the first of the carpet-bag Governors' and quoted the Philadelphia Record on the 'misfortunes of the whole line of political spoilsmen in the South'.
The Portland Daily Press and Wheeling Register ran the Toledo wires on the lynching danger and the removal to Defiance without comment.
